extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and students interested in the methodology and heuristics of mathematical discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Lakatos's methodological criteria for mathematical conjecture formation, proof, refutation, and concept-formation (the logic of 'proofs and refutations'). Useful for guiding how to produce, test, and revise mathematical claims and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not limit enquiry to the first naive conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should our search for content be delimited by the first naive conjecture we stumble upon? Why should the aim of our enquiry be the 'domain of the naive conjecture'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a naive conjecture is discovered by accident, one should be prepared to abandon or replace it with a wider, deeper problem; do not confine investigation to just explaining the accidental domain of the first conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naive conjectures arise by trial-and-error, not genuine induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Naive conjectures are arrived at by trial and error (pre-naive conjectures and refutations) rather than by a pure inductive movement from facts to conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'naive conjecture' as the outcome of earlier conjectures and refutations; compiling longer tables of facts in hope of 'induction' may be wasteful if it obscures heuristic/deductive possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical heuristic = conjectures, proofs, and refutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical heuristic is characterised by conjectures, proofs (or proof-like thought-experiments), and refutations; it is very like scientific heuristic in this structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise cycles of conjecture and refutation rather than assuming a purely deductive or purely inductive route; expect different nature of conjectures, proofs and counterexamples in mathematics versus science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive guessing (proof-generated conjectures) over naive guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: One can start mathematical work not from observation but from deduction: a proof or thought-experiment can generate a conjecture (a 'deductive guessing') without first large-scale observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background knowledge and related propositions to derive plausible conjectures analytically; proofs can precede the naive conjecture and produce deeper, higher-content hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive starting points are unnecessary for proofs and refutations
rubrics_metrics.description: For the logic of proofs and refutations we need no naive conjecture, no inductivist starting point at all: proof can precede the naive conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feel compelled to collect empirical tables before attempting to construct proofs or thought-experiments that yield conjectures and refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish test (analysis) from proof (synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: What looks like a 'proof' (e.g. Cauchy's proof) may actually be a test: drawing consequences to see if they match known truths; analysis (testing) differs from synthesis (proving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a purported proof ask whether it merely draws consequences that are known (corroboration) or whether it constitutes a genuine synthesis; do not mistake corroboration/test-results for logical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5: convert counterexamples by deductive guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 5. If you have counterexamples of any type, try to find, by deductive guessing, a deeper theorem to which they are not counter-examples any longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering counterexamples, seek a deeper, more general theorem that explains and incorporates them (increase the theorem's content) rather than dismissing or excluding the counterexamples ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer proof-generated (theoretical) concepts to naive concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish proof-generated versus naive concepts, and theoretical versus naive classification; concept-formation can be driven by proofs rather than by naive observational grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and refine concepts in light of proof-analysis; theoretical (proof-generated) concepts tend to be more explanatory and robust against counterexamples than naive classifications based only on appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation by concept-stretching as a method (and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutation by concept-stretching, a reappraisal of monster-barring and of the concepts of error and refutation: one may 'stretch' definitions to accommodate or exclude cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concept-stretching carefully: unlimited stretching destroys meaning and truth; mitigated concept-stretching can convert contingent mathematical truth into logical truth—but watch for vacuity and loss of explanatory content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring and monster-adjustment are (anti-)patterns for handling counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to anomalies include monster-barring (excluding counterexamples by definition) and monster-adjustment (reinterpreting objects to fit the theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise these as problematic heuristics: monster-barring/adjustment may restore a theorem but at the cost of ad hoc or linguistically dubious moves; prefer explanatory adjustments that increase content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thought-experiments (proof-thoughtexperiments and test-thoughtexperiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply thought-experiments both for synthesis (proof-thoughtexperiment) and analysis (test-thoughtexperiment) to check conjectures and to attempt proofs without direct empirical enumeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought-experiments can convert refutations into opportunities for proof or can yield proofs that bypass large-scale empirical testing; they are core tools in Lakatos's heuristic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase content by constructing deeper, more explanatory theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive guessing may produce the promised increase in content: constructing a wider conjecture/theorem that explains previously puzzling counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek theorems that not only fit known examples but also offer broader explanatory scope (e.g. generalising Euler's formula by accounting for tunnels, rings, cavities), thereby increasing the 'content' of the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of trivial or uninteresting increases in precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision can increase content but may also produce cheap or pretentious trivialities; there is a balance—'stop when it ceases to be interesting to go on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for meaningful increases in explanatory power when adding technical precision; avoid endlessly technical generalisations that add little insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background knowledge guides conjecture formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems and conjectures grow out of background knowledge; the expectation whose refutation created the problem (e.g. V=E for polygons) often supplies the idea for generalisation without new data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies, familiar cases, and conceptual relations as starting points for conjectures instead of relying only on compiled empirical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis and synthesis may use different lemmas; synthetic theorem should supersede analytic if different
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis (testing) may lead by different lemmas than synthesis (proof); if analytic and synthetic theorems differ, the synthetic theorem should supersede the analytic one since synthesis proves while analysis only tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysis and synthesis diverge, prefer the result of a genuine synthesis/proof as the authoritative theorem, but examine differences to refine understanding and avoid hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate corroboration with proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing consequences from a conjecture that happen to match known truths gives corroboration, not proof—the test may seem to support the conjecture but does not constitute a logical proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require logical derivation and careful argument for claims of proof; treat successful tests as tentative corroboration that motivates further analysis or synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic pluralism: learn and apply both deductive and naive guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher: 'We certainly have to learn both heuristic patterns: deductive guessing is best, but naive guessing is better than no guessing at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate both methods: use deductive (proof-generated) conjecturing when possible, but accept naive/trial-and-error conjectures as a practical fallback or complement.
